Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> HP News 10 | National BoG warns strong El Niño could affect food prices, cocoa and cedi Source : GNA 17 November 2026 5:04am Bank of Ghana Governor, Dr Johnson Asiama ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, Governor of the Bank of Ghana (BoG), Monday warned that an unusually strong El Niño episode could affect agricultural production across West Africa, including Ghana.
He said the Pacific Ocean warming phenomenon, which disrupts global weather patterns, could persist into the first quarter of 2027, with implications for food prices, domestic agricultural output, cocoa production, export earnings, inflation and the exchange rate.
He gave the warning at the opening of the final Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting for 2026 in Accra, where members are expected to review developments during the year and assess whether further adjustments to policy instruments may be necessary.
Urging the Committee to consider weather-related risks in its 133rd meeting, Dr Asiama said an unusually strong El Niño episode could affect agricultural production across West Africa into the first quarter of the following year.
He said the development could have implications for food prices, domestic agricultural output, Ghana’s cocoa production and export earnings, with possible effects on inflation and the exchange rate.
The Governor urged the Committee to provide a comprehensive assessment of the potential transmission channels, their implications for the domestic economic outlook and measures to manage the associated risks effectively.
He also highlighted the broader risks to domestic agriculture, noting that lower production could affect rural incomes, food availability and growth in the agricultural sector.
Dr Asiama emphasised that cocoa, one of Ghana’s major export commodities, remained particularly exposed, as adverse weather conditions could disrupt production and reduce export volumes.
Any shortfall in cocoa output could directly affect export earnings, which had been an important source of strength for the external sector and reserve accumulation, he said.
Beyond the El Niño threat, the MPC, at its 133rd meeting, would consider domestic and external developments, including the global economic outlook, geopolitical developments and commodity prices.
On the domestic front, the Committee would assess the recent uptick in inflation and inflation expectations, developments in the external sector and reserves, and the effectiveness of monetary policy.
It would then make appropriate recommendations on the monetary policy stance as the Bank prepared for 2027.
The Committee is expected to announce its decision at the end of the meeting on Wednesday, November 18.
At its September meeting, the Committee maintained the policy rate at 14 per cent, marking its third consecutive hold after similar decisions in May and July.
This followed reductions from 18 per cent to 15.5 per cent in January and subsequently to 14 per cent in March, amid declining inflation and improving macroeconomic stability.
